rebound-hypoglycaemia.short: A dip in blood glucose early in exercise after carbohydrate eaten 30–60 min before the start: insulin from the meal and the working muscles both pull glucose out of the blood at once. Usually brief.

gastric-emptying.short: How fast the stomach passes food and drink on to the small intestine, where nutrients are absorbed. Fat, fibre, protein and very concentrated drinks slow it down.

exogenous-carbohydrate.short: Carbohydrate from outside the body: drinks, gels and food taken during exercise. Its opposite, endogenous carbohydrate, is the body's own glycogen and the glucose the liver releases.

mouth-rinse.short: Swirling a carbohydrate drink around the mouth for 5–10 s and spitting it out. Sensors in the mouth signal the brain, though nothing is swallowed.

maltodextrin.short: Short chains of glucose made from starch. Much less sweet than sugar; the gut breaks it down and absorbs it as glucose. The base of many sports drinks and gels.

multiple-transportable-carbohydrates.short: A blend of carbohydrates that enter the gut wall through different transporters, usually glucose (or maltodextrin) plus fructose. With two entry routes open, more carbohydrate gets in per hour than with glucose alone.

exogenous-oxidation-rate.short: How many grams of the carbohydrate you swallow are actually burned per minute (or hour). Measured by labelling the drink's carbon and catching the label in breathed-out CO₂.

oxidation-efficiency.short: The share of swallowed carbohydrate that is burned during the exercise: exogenous oxidation rate ÷ intake rate. The rest is still in the gut, stored, or burned later.

gi-symptoms.short: Gastrointestinal (gut) complaints. Upper: nausea, reflux, bloating, stomach fullness. Lower: cramps, wind, urge to go, diarrhoea.

splanchnic-blood-flow.short: Blood flow to the gut, liver, spleen and pancreas. Hard exercise diverts it to the muscles and skin, so the gut gets less.

malabsorption.short: When swallowed carbohydrate isn't absorbed in the small intestine and reaches the large bowel, where bacteria ferment it into gas (hydrogen, measurable in the breath). Causes bloating, wind and diarrhoea.

gut-training.short: Practising eating and drinking during exercise (and eating enough carbohydrate day to day) so the stomach and intestine adapt: less discomfort and, possibly, faster absorption.

carbohydrate-concentration.short: Grams of carbohydrate per 100 mL of drink, written as a percentage: 60 g in 1,000 mL is 6%. Most sports drinks are 6–8%.
